howMuch.heading: How Much Protein Do You Need Per Day?
howMuch.intro: Daily protein needs scale with body weight, activity level and goal. The table below shows commonly recommended ranges in grams of protein per kilogram of body weight.

byWeight.heading: Daily Protein Needs by Body Weight
byWeight.intro: Looking for a quick answer for your weight? The table below shows daily protein targets at common body weights — a lower range for general health and a higher range if you train regularly or are dieting to lose fat.
byWeight.note: For a target tailored to your exact weight, age and goal, use the calculator above.

weightLoss.heading: Protein Intake for Weight Loss
weightLoss.body: When you eat fewer calories than you burn, your body can break down muscle for energy alongside fat. A higher protein intake — typically 1.6g to 2.4g per kilogram of body weight — helps preserve lean muscle during a cut, keeps hunger in check thanks to protein's satiety effect, and slightly raises the number of calories burned digesting food.

muscleGain.heading: Protein Intake for Muscle Gain
muscleGain.body: Building muscle requires a calorie surplus, consistent resistance training, and enough protein to fuel muscle repair — generally 1.6g to 2.2g per kilogram of body weight per day. Spreading protein evenly across 3–4 meals, rather than loading it into one meal, gives your body a steady supply of amino acids for muscle protein synthesis throughout the day.

women.heading: Protein Intake for Women
women.intro: Protein needs for women follow the same weight-based ranges as men, with a few life stages that call for extra intake. Pregnancy and breastfeeding both raise protein needs to support the baby's growth, while adequate protein after menopause helps offset the natural decline in muscle and bone density.
women.note: General guidance only — pregnant or breastfeeding women should confirm intake with their doctor or midwife.

glp1.heading: Protein Intake on GLP-1 Medications (Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro)
glp1.intro: GLP-1 medications suppress appetite, so total food intake — and with it, protein intake — often drops sharply. Because a large share of weight lost on these medications can come from muscle if protein is neglected, many prescribers now recommend prioritizing protein-rich foods first at every meal and aiming for the higher end of the standard range (around 1.2g–1.6g per kilogram of body weight, or more if you also strength train).
tips: Eat protein first, before carbs or vegetables, at each meal.
Favor high-protein, low-volume foods (eggs, Greek yogurt, whey, paneer) since appetite and portion sizes are reduced.
Pair with light resistance training where possible to help protect muscle mass.
glp1.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice. Always follow the guidance of the doctor managing your prescription.

items.q: How much protein do I need per day?
items.a: Most adults need between 0.8g and 2.2g of protein per kilogram of body weight per day, depending on activity level and goals. Sedentary adults need less, while those building muscle or in a calorie deficit need more to preserve lean mass.

items.q: How much protein for muscle gain?
items.a: To build muscle, aim for roughly 1.6g to 2.2g of protein per kilogram of body weight daily, combined with resistance training and a slight calorie surplus.

items.q: How much protein should I eat to lose weight?
items.a: When cutting calories, a higher protein intake of around 1.8g to 2.4g per kilogram of body weight helps preserve muscle mass and keeps you fuller for longer.

items.q: Does protein intake change on Ozempic, Wegovy or Mounjaro?
items.a: GLP-1 medications reduce appetite, so total food intake drops. Prioritizing protein at each meal helps offset muscle loss during rapid weight loss. Always confirm your target with the doctor managing your prescription.

items.q: Is it bad to eat too much protein?
items.a: For most healthy adults, higher protein intakes within these ranges are safe. Spread your intake across 3-4 meals a day for the best absorption and results.

items.q: How much protein do vegetarians need?
items.a: Vegetarians need the same amount of protein as anyone else for their weight, activity level and goal — the difference is sourcing it from foods like paneer, lentils, tofu, Greek yogurt, eggs and dairy instead of meat. Combining a few plant sources across the day (e.g. lentils with rice or dal with paneer) covers the full range of essential amino acids.

items.q: Is there a vegan protein calculator?
items.a: Yes — after calculating your protein target, switch to the Vegan option under "Diet preference" in the results to see a sample day built entirely from plant-based sources like tofu, lentils, chickpeas, peanut butter, soy milk and plant protein powder that adds up to your target.

items.q: Do older adults need more protein?
items.a: Yes. Adults over 60 typically need more protein than younger adults — often 1.2g to 1.6g per kilogram of body weight — to help offset age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia) and maintain strength and bone health.

items.q: How much protein should I eat per meal?
items.a: Most people do best aiming for 25g to 40g of protein per meal, spread across 3-4 meals a day. This keeps muscle protein synthesis elevated throughout the day rather than concentrating intake into a single large meal.

items.q: Is 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight the right target?
items.a: 1g per pound of body weight (about 2.2g per kilogram) sits at the high end of the evidence-based range and works well for lean, heavily-training individuals. Most people — including those simply maintaining muscle or losing fat — do just as well with 0.7g to 1g per pound (1.6g to 2.2g per kg).

protein-for-men.heading: Protein Intake for Men: How Much Do You Need?
protein-for-men.lead: Most men need 0.8–1.0 g of protein per kg of body weight for general health, and 1.6–2.2 g/kg to build muscle or lose fat. For an 80 kg (176 lb) man, that is roughly 130–175 g of protein per day when training regularly.
paragraphs: Because men on average carry more lean body mass, their absolute protein needs are higher than women's at the same body weight. A sedentary 80 kg man covers basic needs with 64–80 g per day, but that minimum only prevents deficiency — it is not optimal for body composition, strength or appetite control.

If you lift weights or play sports, research supports 1.6–2.2 g/kg per day. Spread it over three to four meals of 30–45 g each, keep one protein-rich meal within a few hours of training, and build your plates around lean meat, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes and tofu before reaching for supplements.
bullets: Sedentary: 0.8–1.0 g/kg per day (64–80 g for an 80 kg man)
Muscle gain: 1.6–2.2 g/kg per day, paired with resistance training
Fat loss: 1.8–2.4 g/kg per day to protect muscle in a calorie deficit
Over 50: at least 1.2 g/kg per day to counter age-related muscle loss

protein-for-seniors.heading: Protein for Seniors: Needs After 50, 60 and 70
protein-for-seniors.lead: Adults over 60 generally need 1.0–1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight per day — more than younger adults — and 1.2–1.5 g/kg when recovering from illness or fighting age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia).
paragraphs: With age, muscles respond less efficiently to protein — a phenomenon called anabolic resistance. That is why geriatric nutrition experts recommend 1.0–1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight for healthy adults over 60, rising to 1.2–1.5 g/kg during illness or recovery, compared with 0.8 g/kg for younger adults.

Distribution matters as much as the total: aim for 25–30 g of protein at each main meal, including a leucine-rich source such as dairy, eggs, fish, meat or soy. Combining that intake with simple resistance exercise two to three times a week is the best-proven way to slow sarcopenia.
bullets: Healthy adults over 60: 1.0–1.2 g/kg per day
Illness or recovery: 1.2–1.5 g/kg per day (ask your doctor)
Per meal: 25–30 g, including a leucine-rich source
Pair protein with strength exercise 2–3 times a week

protein-for-teenagers.heading: Protein for Teenagers: How Much During Growth?
protein-for-teenagers.lead: Teenagers need roughly 0.85–1.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day to support growth, and active teen athletes can benefit from 1.2–1.6 g/kg. Balanced meals cover these amounts — supplements are rarely necessary.
paragraphs: Protein needs per kilogram peak during the adolescent growth spurt, when the body is building bone, muscle and organ tissue at its fastest rate. Regular meals built around milk, yogurt, eggs, meat, fish, beans and nuts comfortably meet these needs for most teenagers without any special products.

Teen athletes training most days can aim for 1.2–1.6 g/kg, ideally as 20–40 g of protein per meal plus a protein-rich snack after practice. Keep the focus on real food first; protein powder is a convenience, not a requirement, and extreme diets during growth years can do lasting harm.
bullets: General teens: 0.85–1.0 g/kg per day, from regular balanced meals
Teen athletes: 1.2–1.6 g/kg per day across 3–4 meals
Per meal: about 20–40 g depending on body size
Food first — protein supplements are rarely needed in adolescence

protein-during-pregnancy.heading: Protein During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding
protein-during-pregnancy.lead: Pregnancy raises protein needs to roughly 1.1 g per kg of body weight per day — about 25 g extra compared with before — and breastfeeding keeps needs similarly elevated. Always confirm your personal target with your doctor or midwife.
paragraphs: Protein requirements rise mainly in the second and third trimesters, as the baby, placenta and maternal tissues grow. Guidelines translate to roughly 1.1 g per kg per day — about 70–100 g for many women, or 25 g more than pre-pregnancy needs — and breastfeeding keeps requirements at a similar level.

Meet the target with foods that also supply iron, choline, iodine and calcium: eggs, dairy, low-mercury cooked fish, poultry, legumes, tofu and nuts. Avoid high-dose protein supplements unless your doctor or midwife recommends them, and treat this page as general information, not medical advice.
bullets: Second and third trimester: about 1.1 g/kg per day (~25 g extra)
Breastfeeding: needs stay elevated at a similar level
Choose protein foods rich in iron, choline and calcium
Discuss supplements and personal targets with your doctor or midwife

best-time-to-eat-protein.heading: Best Time to Eat Protein: Timing, Spacing and Workouts
best-time-to-eat-protein.lead: Total daily protein matters far more than timing, but spreading it across 3–4 meals of 25–40 g each — including one within a few hours of training — gets the most muscle protein synthesis from the same grams.
paragraphs: Studies comparing protein timing consistently find that total daily intake is the strongest driver of muscle growth and retention. The post-workout “anabolic window” is much wider than once believed — eating protein within a couple of hours before or after training works about equally well.

Distribution still helps: muscle protein synthesis is maximized around 0.4 g/kg per meal, roughly 25–40 g for most people. Spreading intake over 3–4 meals, adding protein at breakfast where most people eat the least, and taking 20–40 g of slow-digesting protein such as casein or Greek yogurt before bed round out an evidence-based routine.
bullets: Hit your daily total first — timing is a refinement, not the foundation
Aim for 25–40 g of protein per meal, 3–4 times a day
Eat a protein-rich meal within ~2 hours before or after training
Slow protein (casein, Greek yogurt) before bed supports overnight recovery

protein-shakes-per-day.heading: How Many Protein Shakes a Day? Do You Need Powder?
protein-shakes-per-day.lead: Protein shakes are a convenience, not a requirement. If whole foods leave you 30–60 g short of your daily target, one or two shakes a day is a practical way to close the gap — more than that rarely adds value.
paragraphs: A shake is simply food in liquid form: one scoop of whey, casein, soy or pea protein provides about 25–30 g. If you already reach your daily target from meals, extra shakes add nothing but calories; if you are consistently short, one or two shakes are an easy, inexpensive fix.

Whole foods bring fiber, micronutrients and more satiety per calorie, so keep shakes in a gap-filling role. Choose third-party-tested powders, watch added sugars in ready-to-drink products, and consider whey isolate or plant-based options if regular dairy upsets your stomach.
bullets: Zero shakes needed if meals already cover your protein target
1–2 shakes a day is a sensible practical maximum for most people
One scoop of powder ≈ 25–30 g of protein
Prefer third-party-tested powders and watch added sugar

protein-for-diabetics.heading: Protein Intake for Diabetics and Blood Sugar Control
protein-for-diabetics.lead: For most people with type 2 diabetes and healthy kidneys, 1.0–1.5 g of protein per kg of body weight supports satiety and steadier blood sugar. Kidney disease changes the math — individual targets belong with your doctor.
paragraphs: Protein barely raises blood glucose, and it slows the absorption of carbohydrates eaten in the same meal. Distributing 25–35 g of protein across each meal can therefore flatten glucose spikes and improve satiety — particularly useful for weight management in type 2 diabetes.

For people with normal kidney function, 1.0–1.5 g/kg per day is generally considered safe and beneficial. In diabetic kidney disease, protein targets must be individualized — often closer to 0.8 g/kg — so review your intake with your doctor or dietitian before making significant changes.
bullets: Normal kidney function: 1.0–1.5 g/kg per day is generally appropriate
25–35 g of protein per meal helps blunt glucose spikes
Favor lean and plant proteins: fish, poultry, legumes, tofu, dairy
Kidney disease: targets must be set with your doctor or dietitian

protein-deficiency-signs.heading: Protein Deficiency: Signs You Are Not Eating Enough
protein-deficiency-signs.lead: Common signs of low protein intake include shrinking strength and muscle, constant hunger, slow recovery, hair shedding, brittle nails and frequent illness. Most adults stay safe above 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight per day.
paragraphs: True protein deficiency is rare in high-income countries, but suboptimal intake is common — especially among older adults, chronic dieters and people who skip meals. Early signs include losing strength, feeling hungry again soon after eating, slow wound healing and catching infections more often.

Hair shedding, brittle nails and, in severe cases, swelling (edema) reflect protein's structural and fluid-balance roles. The fix is straightforward: calculate your personal target with the calculator above, then anchor every meal with a palm-sized protein source. See a doctor if symptoms persist — several have non-dietary causes.
bullets: Loss of muscle and strength despite normal activity
Constant hunger and cravings shortly after meals
Hair shedding, brittle nails and slow-healing skin
Frequent minor illnesses and sluggish recovery from training

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.metaDescription: How Protein Intake Calculator handles your data: calculations stay in your browser, no personal data is stored, and Google AdSense may use cookies to serve ads.
privacy.intro: Your privacy matters. This page explains what information proteinintakecalculators.online collects, how it is used, and the choices you have. The short version: the calculator runs entirely in your browser, we don't ask for or store personal data, and the only third-party cookies come from advertising.

dataCollection.heading: Information This Site Collects
paragraphs: The protein calculator runs entirely in your browser. The details you enter — age, weight, height, activity level and goal — are used only to compute your result on your device. They are never saved, transmitted or shared.
This site has no user accounts, no sign-up forms and no newsletter, so we never ask for your name, email address or any other personal information.

advertising.heading: Advertising and Google AdSense
paragraphs: This site uses Google AdSense to display ads. Third-party vendors, including Google, use cookies to serve ads based on your prior visits to this website or other websites.

Google's use of advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads to you based on your visits to this site and/or other sites on the internet. Where required by law (for example in the European Economic Area and the UK), ads are only personalized with your consent.
You can opt out of personalized advertising, or learn more about how Google uses data, via the links below:

links.partnerSites: How Google uses information from sites that use its services
links.aboutAds: www.aboutads.info — opt out of personalized advertising

cookies.heading: Cookies
paragraphs: A cookie is a small text file stored by your browser. This site does not set cookies of its own; the only cookies you may encounter here are set by advertising partners as described above. You can block or delete cookies at any time in your browser settings — the calculator works fully without them.

hosting.heading: Hosting and Log Data
paragraphs: Like almost every website, the servers that host this site may automatically record basic technical data such as your IP address, browser type and the pages you visit. These logs are used only to keep the site secure and running and are not combined with any other data to identify you.

children.heading: Children's Privacy
paragraphs: This site provides general nutrition information and is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect personal information from anyone, including children.

changes.heading: Changes to This Policy
paragraphs: We may update this policy from time to time, for example when advertising partners change. The latest version will always be available on this page, with the date above updated accordingly.

about.title: About This Site
about.metaDescription: What Protein Intake Calculator is for, how the recommendations are calculated, and how the site is funded.
about.intro: proteinintakecalculators.online is a free tool that helps you work out how much protein you need each day — whether your goal is losing weight, building muscle or simply staying healthy.

mission.heading: What This Site Is For
paragraphs: Protein advice online is often contradictory: one article says 0.8 grams per kilogram, the next says you need double that. Our goal is to cut through the noise and give you a clear, personalized number in seconds, together with practical guides for real-life situations — weight loss, muscle gain, pregnancy, vegetarian diets and more.
Everything on this site is free and works without an account. You enter your details, you get your range, and nothing you type ever leaves your browser.

methodology.heading: How the Numbers Are Calculated
paragraphs: The calculator is built on the Mifflin-St Jeor equation and on daily protein ranges used by dietitians and strength coaches — roughly 0.8 to 2.2 grams per kilogram of body weight, depending on your goal, age and activity level.
The full method is explained step by step right on the calculator page, so you can always see exactly how your result was produced. No guesswork, no black box.

funding.heading: How the Site Is Funded
paragraphs: The site is funded by advertising, which is what keeps every tool and guide free. Ads never influence the recommendations — those come from published nutrition research and are the same for everyone.

medical.heading: Not Medical Advice
paragraphs: Everything here is general nutrition information, not medical advice. If you are pregnant, managing a condition such as diabetes or kidney disease, or taking medication that affects your appetite, talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian before changing your protein intake.
